new_statements.quote: The placement of stress (tɬə ɬinnwi k’ellis də gila’is) in miluk has not been previously described. As with many, if not most languages with stress systems, there are tendencies but with many exceptions. Stress tends to be assigned to the penultimate syllable in a word, as in (2.31) and (2.32). [...] This is indicative of a secondary-stress system. Specifically, primary stress appears to go on the penultimate syllable, with secondary stresses branching leftward in what typically appear to be trochaic feet, as in (2.33) and (2.34) above. The acoustic differences between primary and secondary stress are not known due to the limitations of the primary sources.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress tends to fall on the penultimate syllable of the word (e.g. híich’i 'one', pxwáanis 'bruise', adzú’an 'eight', pəxáawəl, mich’lé’wəs), based on Jacobs' acute-accent markings in elicited words and texts; the author presents it as a tendency with many unexplained exceptions, not an exceptionless rule. Main acoustic correlate is duration (Douglas-Tavani & Shirtz n.d.); Jacobs 1939:18 described stressed syllables as higher-pitched (level or falling) and longer.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stresses branch leftward from the penult in trochaic feet (e.g. gyínwuts’úwa, híchhijínai); acoustic difference between primary and secondary not determinable from the archival sources.
new_statements.exceptions: Many deviations in connected speech (exx. 2.40-2.43) left unexplained; words with every syllable marked stressed attributed to storytelling/phrase-level prominence (2.35); clitics are inside the prosodic word for the trochaic count but are dispreferred as stress hosts even when penultimate (2.44-2.45), though they can bear stress, especially in 'symbiotic clitic clusters' (2.46-2.47); enclitic =wu interacts with stress assignment.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement; evidence is Jacobs' 1930s transcriptions of Annie Miner Peterson (isolated elicited words, ex. 2.31, and connected text, ex. 2.32ff) plus one phonograph recording; author notes sentence-phrase (intonation-unit) level pressures likely influence stress marks in texts. Language is dormant; description is archival-philological.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes miluk tɬiis (Miluk, Lower Coquille; glottocode milu1241, ISO iml) as recorded almost entirely from one speaker, Annie Miner Peterson, by Melville Jacobs in 1933-34; not Hanis Coos (coos1249), which the author treats as a separate language (hanis tɬii'iis).

sources.note: Ch.2 §2.3 'Stress' (pp.60-68): §2.3.1 acoustic correlates (duration strongest, per Douglas-Tavani & Shirtz n.d; Jacobs 1939:18 'stress-accent' = higher tone, longer); §2.3.2 placement 'not previously described': stress tends to fall on the penultimate syllable, with secondary stresses on leftward trochees; many exceptions; clitics count in the prosodic word but are dispreferred as stress hosts; phrase-level intonation likely interferes in connected speech.
